sections.title: Story & History
text: From ancient fields to modern times, sugarcane has been part of human civilisations for thousands of years. It has sweetened celebrations, strengthened communities, and stood the test of time.
Originating in New Guinea, sugarcane spread across Asia, the Middle East, Europe and the world. It played a vital role in trade, economies, and cultures for centuries.

sections.title: The Life Cycle of Sugarcane
sections.intro: From a cutting in the soil to the glass in your hand – and back to the soil again. Turn the pages.

pages.title: Planting

image.alt: Young sugarcane plant with its roots

pages.caption: A new plant from an old cane
text: Sugarcane is not grown from seed. Short pieces of a mature stalk, called setts, are laid in rich, moist soil.
Each joint carries a sleeping bud that wakes, sends down roots and pushes up a fresh green shoot.

pages.title: Growing
pages.caption: Sun, water and patience
text: Warm sun, plenty of water and patient care. The young shoots grow into tall, leafy canes, often taller than a person.
Joint by joint the stalk climbs, its long leaves rustling in the field.

pages.title: Ripening

image.alt: A tall field of ripe sugarcane

pages.caption: Ten to fourteen months in the field
text: Over 10–14 months the canes fill with sweet juice. The stalks grow firm and heavy.
The cane is ready when its sweetness is at its very best.

pages.title: Harvest
pages.caption: Cut low, where it is sweetest
text: The ripe canes are cut close to the ground, where the juice is sweetest, and the leaves are stripped away.
The roots stay in the soil and send up new canes for the next harvest.

pages.title: Bundled & Carried
pages.caption: Fresh from the field
text: The canes are tied into bundles and carried away fresh.
Cane juice is best when the cane is freshly cut, so it does not wait around.

pages.title: Into the Press
pages.caption: The rollers turn
text: Each cane is washed and fed through the press. The rollers crush it and squeeze out the sweet green-gold juice.

pages.title: A Fresh Glass

image.alt: A glass of fresh sugarcane juice

pages.caption: Pure, fresh, nothing added
text: Poured straight into the glass, perhaps with a squeeze of lemon, a little ginger or a sprig of mint.
This is the part we love most – handing it to you.

pages.title: Many Good Things
pages.caption: One plant, many gifts
text: The same sweet juice, boiled and worked in different ways, gives us much more than a drink.

pages.title: From Fibre to Plates
pages.caption: Nothing goes to waste
text: After pressing, the dry fibre left behind is called bagasse.
It is made into plates, cups and paper, and burned as fuel – nothing goes to waste.

pages.title: Back to the Soil
pages.caption: The field is ready again
text: Used plates, leaves and fibre break down into rich compost that feeds the earth.
The soil is ready for new setts to be planted.

sections.title: Sugarcane in Our Culture
text: A part of festivals, traditions, rituals and celebrations. It connects generations and brings people together.
At harvest festivals whole canes are tied at the door, shared with neighbours and chewed by children in the sun. At weddings and temple offerings it stands for a sweet, plentiful life ahead.
Every glass we press carries a little of that same feeling: something simple, fresh and shared.
